summary: A 1975 comment on the IMP and host protocol changes of RFC 687 and RFC 690, proposing a solution to the problem of the combined length of the IMP and host leaders. See also RFC 696.

eli5.summary: Message headers from two layers added up to too much. This note proposes a way to keep them from getting too long.

questions: comments on imp host protocol changes
what is the imp host protocol
subtitle: A 1975 note arguing that a 104-bit IMP leader is better than changing every host's protocol leader.

tldr.problem: The changes in RFC 687 would make the combined IMP and Host leaders 120 bits, which is not a multiple of both 8 and 36 bits.
tldr.mechanism: Stephen Wolfe suggests making the new IMP leader 104 bits instead of 80, with rules that let the IMP ignore the last 8 bits, and also proposes a new IMP-to-Host message carrying Host names and addresses.
tldr.outcome: This is a short comment, not a specification. It argues that changing the IMP program is faster and cheaper than forcing changes in all hosts.

today: RFC 692 updates RFC 690; the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and shows no later RFC replacing it.

sections.title: The Leader Length Problem
sections.content:
Wolfe, at UCLA CCN, finds the changes proposed in RFC 687 and the comments in RFC 690 basically reasonable. The major problem, pointed out by Postel, is that the combined length of the IMP and Host leaders becomes 120 bits, which is not a multiple of both 8 and 36 bits.

One suggestion is to lengthen the host-to-host protocol leader by 24 bits, for a total of 144 bits. But the only compatible way would be for the IMP to insert or delete the extra 24 bits when converting to or from the old format, and Wolfe says the problems with that are obvious.
sections.eli5: Two headers stuck together come out to a size that does not fit nicely in either of the two kinds of computer word. Making one longer by a lot is messy.

sections.title: A 104-Bit IMP Leader
sections.content:
Wolfe prefers to change the new IMP leader itself, to 104 bits instead of 80. He accepts that 104 is not a multiple of an IMP word, but says it should not be difficult if four rules are followed.

  • The last 8 bits are never used to convey information.
  • The network is not required to pass them from source to destination, or to return them to the source.
  • For message types other than zero (irregular messages), the IMP may send 96, 104 or 112 bits of data, at its convenience.
  • If desired, 96 or 112 could instead be the new leader length for irregular messages.

His reasoning is that it must be faster and cheaper to change the IMP program to handle a 104-bit leader than to force additional changes in all hosts using the standard protocol.
sections.eli5: Make the one piece the network controls a bit longer, and agree that the last few bits are just filler. That is easier than asking everyone to change.

sections.title: A Host Name Table Message
sections.content:
Wolfe also suggests a new type of IMP-to-Host message. It would carry a table of Host names (character strings that people type) and Host network addresses.

The message or messages would be sent to the Host after each interface reset. Alternatively, it could be a response to a new Host-to-IMP request for this information.
sections.eli5: The network would hand each computer a phone book of names and numbers when it connects, or whenever it asks for one.
